tooley.q: A standard logic gate manufactured in 1981 is likely to be supplied in a:
tooley.explain: In the 1980s, DIL (Dual-In-Line) was the most common package style for standard logic ICs.
tooley.detail: Before surface-mount technology became widespread in the late 1980s, almost every standard logic IC used a DIL (Dual-In-Line) package with two rows of through-hole pins, which was easy to hand-solder and easy to plug into a socket for repair.

tooley.q: A standard logic gate is a typical example of:
tooley.explain: A single logic gate contains only a few transistors → it belongs to the smallest integration scale, SSI.
tooley.detail: Scale of integration is classified by the number of equivalent logic gates on one chip: SSI (Small Scale Integration) holds only a handful of individual gates, MSI (Medium) holds tens to around a hundred gates, LSI (Large) reaches into the thousands, and VLSI (Very Large) contains millions of transistors or more, as in a modern microprocessor.

tooley.q: Which one of the following scales of integration is the largest:
tooley.explain: Order of increasing density: SSI < MSI < LSI < VLSI; of the 3 choices, LSI is the largest.
tooley.detail: The four integration scales always follow the fixed order SSI, MSI, LSI, VLSI, from fewest to most logic gates. Remembering this order makes it quick to answer any 'which scale is larger' question without needing to recall the exact gate count of each level.

tooley.q: A microprocessor is an example of:
tooley.explain: A microprocessor contains millions of transistors → it belongs to the very large scale of integration, VLSI.
tooley.detail: A modern microprocessor packs anywhere from several million to billions of transistors onto a single chip, far beyond the few thousand gates typical of LSI, so it is always classed as VLSI (Very Large Scale Integration). This is exactly the technology that allows an entire central processing unit to shrink onto one chip instead of filling a large circuit board as in early computers.

tooley.q: Compared with DIP packaging, PLCC offers:
opts: more pins in the same size
tooley.explain: PLCC (Plastic Leaded Chip Carrier) allows more pins in a more compact area than DIP.
tooley.detail: PLCC places pins along all four sides of a square package instead of just two rows as in DIP, so for the same footprint area it fits considerably more pins. The trade-off is that PLCC is harder to hand-solder and usually needs a dedicated socket or surface-mount soldering equipment.

tooley.q: Which IC packaging technology requires the chip to always be soldered in place:
tooley.explain: SOIC is a surface-mount package that is always soldered directly to the board, not plugged into a socket like DIL/PGA.
tooley.detail: SOIC (Small Outline IC) belongs to the surface-mount package family, with gull-wing leads soldered directly onto the copper pads of the printed circuit board, with no separate socketed version the way DIL or PGA have. This makes SOIC considerably more compact but also harder to remove and re-seat during repair.

tooley.q: Which of the following IC packaging technologies was the earliest to be used:
tooley.explain: Ceramic DIP is the earliest commercial IC package of the three choices.
tooley.detail: In the history of IC packaging, ceramic DIP dates back to the 1960s, well before the cheaper plastic DIP that followed it and before surface-mount packages such as QFP or PLCC, which only became common from the late 1970s onward as the demand for higher component density grew.

tooley.q: The connections from the pads on an integrated circuit die are:
opts: welded to the internal connecting wires
soldered to the internal connecting wires
crimped to the internal connecting wires
tooley.explain: Wire bonding attaches gold/aluminium wires from the pad to the lead frame by ultrasonic/thermal welding, not by ordinary soldering.
tooley.detail: Wire-bonding uses an extremely thin gold or aluminium wire, with each end attached to a pad on the die and to the lead frame using heat combined with pressure and ultrasonic energy, forming a true metal-diffusion weld rather than a layer of solder the way ordinary board-level soldering works.

tooley.q: An IC bus transceiver containing 64 logic gates and buffers is an example of:
tooley.explain: A few tens up to about 100 logic gates corresponds to medium-scale integration, MSI.
tooley.detail: 64 logic gates sit comfortably within the tens-to-around-a-hundred gate range that defines MSI (Medium Scale Integration), well above a single standalone gate (SSI) but far below the thousands of gates found in LSI.

tooley.q: Production tests are performed on an integrated circuit wafer:
opts: after being cut into individual devices
only after the device has been fitted to a board
before being cut into individual devices
tooley.explain: The wafer is tested (wafer probing) while still whole, before the dicing step.
tooley.detail: Testing while the wafer is still intact (wafer probing) lets defective die be identified immediately with automated electrical probes, avoiding the costly packaging step for chips that were already faulty at the fabrication stage. Dicing only happens after the good and bad die have been clearly marked.

tooley.q: Each individual integrated circuit produced from a wafer is known as a:
tooley.explain: The standard term for an individual chip cut from a wafer is a 'die'.
tooley.detail: A semiconductor wafer holds hundreds to thousands of copies of the same circuit; each individual copy, once cut out, is called a 'die' (plural 'dice' or 'dies'). Only after that die is packaged into a plastic or ceramic case with a lead frame does the product become a finished IC.

tooley.q: A standard TTL logic gate has a fan-out of:
tooley.explain: Standard TTL has a nominal fan-out of 10 (it can drive up to 10 TTL inputs of the same family).
tooley.detail: Fan-out limits how many same-family logic inputs a single output can safely drive, since each input draws a small amount of current from that output. Exceeding 10 TTL inputs on one standard TTL output can pull the high-level voltage below the logic-1 recognition threshold of the following gates, causing intermittent logic errors that are hard to trace.

tooley.q: The equivalent number of standard input loads imposed by the input of a logic circuit is known as:
tooley.explain: This is exactly the definition of fan-in.
tooley.detail: Fan-in and fan-out are easy to confuse because they sound similar but measure two different directions: fan-out measures an output's capacity to SUPPLY load, while fan-in measures how much load an input PLACES on the source driving it. A standard input of the same logic family always has a fan-in of 1 by definition.

tooley.q: Another name for a multiplexer is:
tooley.explain: A multiplexer is often called a 'data selector' because it selects 1 of several data sources for a single output.
tooley.detail: The name 'data selector' actually describes a multiplexer's function more accurately than the word 'multiplex' itself might suggest: the circuit does not blend several signals together, it simply SELECTS exactly one of several input data sources to pass through to a single output, based on the binary code on its select lines.

tooley.q: A four-to-one multiplexer has:
tooley.explain: n select lines are needed to distinguish 2ⁿ input channels; with 4 channels, n = 2.
tooley.detail: The formula n=log₂(N) applies to every multiplexer: there must be enough select lines for their binary code to number all N input data channels. With 4 channels, 2 select lines are needed because 2²=4; with 8 channels, 3 lines are needed because 2³=8, and so on as the channel count grows.

tooley.q: Additional enable inputs and outputs are provided in some encoders in order to permit:
tooley.explain: The enable pins allow several encoder ICs to be cascaded to expand the number of encoded inputs.
tooley.detail: A single encoder IC can only encode a fixed number of inputs by design. The enable input/output pins allow several encoder ICs to be cascaded together, where a lower-priority stage is only allowed to operate once the higher-priority stage signals, through its own enable output, that none of its inputs are currently active.

tooley.q: The logic circuit arrangement shown in Figure A2.10 is:
tooley.explain: 2 input lines select exactly 1 of 4 output lines (Y0-Y3): this is the structure of a 2-to-4 decoder, using NAND gates to produce active-LOW outputs.

tooley.q: The logic device shown in Figure A2.11 is:
tooley.explain: The pin layout matches the 74148 IC exactly: an 8-to-3 line priority encoder.

tooley.q: The pins on a DIL packaged integrated circuit are numbered:
tooley.explain: Standard JEDEC convention: viewed from the top, pins are numbered anti-clockwise starting from pin 1 (the corner with the notch/dot marker).

tooley.q: Which one of the following classes of semiconductor device is most susceptible to static voltages:
tooley.explain: A VLSI microprocessor uses MOS technology with an extremely thin oxide layer at the transistor gate: far more sensitive to electrostatic discharge (ESD) than bipolar devices (BJT/SCR).

tooley.q: What type of package is used for the integrated circuit shown in Figure A2.28?
tooley.explain: Gull-wing leads surface-mounted on two sides with a compact size: characteristic of the SOIC package.

tooley.q: Which one of the following gives the function of the device shown in Figure A2.30?
tooley.explain: 8 data inputs (D0-D7), 3 select lines (A, B, C), 1 output (Y) and an inverted complementary output (W): this is the structure of the 74151 IC, an 8-to-1 multiplexer.

tooley.q: Which one of the following gives the function of IC1 in Figure A2.31?
tooley.explain: IC1 is the symbol of a comparator op-amp between the analog input signal and the sawtooth wave from the ramp generator: the classic structure of a single-slope ADC.

floyd.q: A half-adder adds two binary bits.
floyd.explain: True by the definition of a half adder.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #1
floyd.detail: The half-adder is the simplest adder circuit, handling exactly 2 input bits (A, B) with no carry-in from a previous stage, so it can only be used for the lowest bit position (LSB) when adding two multi-bit numbers.

floyd.q: A half-adder has a carry output only.
floyd.explain: A half adder has 2 outputs: sum (Σ) AND carry, not just carry.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #2
floyd.detail: A half-adder always produces BOTH outputs: the sum (Σ=A XOR B) and the carry-out (Cout=A AND B). Missing either output would not be enough information to add correctly, since the sum bit and the carry bit carry two entirely different meanings in binary addition.

floyd.q: A full adder adds two bits and produces two outputs.
floyd.explain: A full adder adds THREE inputs (2 data bits + 1 carry-in Cin), not just 2 bits.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #3
floyd.detail: The key difference between a half-adder and a full-adder is that the full-adder has an EXTRA Cin (carry-in) input to receive the carry bit from a lower stage. This is what allows full-adders to be chained together to add binary numbers of any bit length.

floyd.q: A full-adder can be realized only by using 2-input XOR gates.
floyd.explain: A full adder needs both XOR AND AND/OR to produce the carry-out, not just XOR.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #4
floyd.detail: XOR alone correctly computes only the SUM bit (Σ=A⊕B⊕Cin), but it cannot by itself produce the correct CARRY-OUT, since the carry-out depends on AT LEAST TWO of the three input bits being 1 together, a condition that needs AND and OR gates as well to express.

floyd.q: When the input bits are both 1 and the input carry bit is 1, the sum output of a full adder is 1.
floyd.explain: 1+1+1 = 11₂ → sum (Σ) = 1, carry out (Cout) = 1: correct, the sum is 1.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #5
floyd.detail: When all 3 full-adder inputs (A, B, Cin) are 1, the arithmetic sum is 1+1+1=3, written as the 2-bit binary value 11. The low bit of this result (=1) is exactly Σ, and the high bit (=1) is exactly Cout, matching the statement.

floyd.q: The output of a comparator is 0 when the two binary inputs given are equal.
floyd.explain: When two numbers are equal, the comparator's 'A = B' output is active (usually 1/HIGH), not 0.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #6
floyd.detail: A standard magnitude comparator always has 3 separate outputs: A>B, A

floyd.q: A decoder detects the presence of a specified combination of input bits.
floyd.explain: True by the basic function of a decoder.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #7
floyd.detail: A decoder is essentially a 'pattern recognition' circuit: it watches the input lines and activates exactly ONE corresponding output line only when the input bit combination matches the code that output represents, while every other output stays inactive.

floyd.q: The 4-line-to-10-line decoder and the 1-of-10 decoder are two different types.
floyd.explain: These are actually the SAME kind of device with two different names, not two different kinds.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #8
floyd.detail: '4-line-to-10-line decoder' describes the decoder by its PHYSICAL number of input/output lines (4 binary-coded inputs, 10 outputs), while '1-of-10 decoder' describes its FUNCTION (selecting exactly 1 of 10 outputs). Both names refer to the exact same familiar BCD-to-decimal decoder IC, not two different designs.

floyd.q: An encoder essentially performs a reverse decoder function.
floyd.explain: True: an encoder and a decoder are two opposite functions.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #9
floyd.detail: A decoder takes a compact binary code and activates exactly one of several corresponding outputs; an encoder does the OPPOSITE, taking an active signal on one of several inputs and producing the compact binary code corresponding to that input. These two circuits commonly appear as a pair in keyboard systems and address encoding.

floyd.q: A multiplexer is a logic circuit that allows digital information from a single source to be routed onto several lines.
floyd.explain: This describes a DEMULTIPLEXER (1 input, many outputs); a multiplexer does the OPPOSITE: many input sources, one selected output line.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · True/False #10
floyd.detail: Multiplexers and demultiplexers are often confused because their names sound similar but their functions are exact opposites. A multiplexer SELECTS 1 of MANY input sources to route to a single output (many-in, one-out); a demultiplexer DISTRIBUTES a single input source to 1 of MANY outputs (one-in, many-out), which is exactly what the question describes.

floyd.q: A half-adder is characterized by
floyd.explain: Half adder: 2 inputs (A, B), 2 outputs (Σ, Cout).
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #1
floyd.detail: The four input/output count combinations among the options are easy to mix up without a clear picture of the definition. The safest approach is to visualise the block diagram: a half-adder has exactly 2 arrows going in (A, B) and 2 arrows going out (Σ, Cout), no more and no less.

floyd.q: A full-adder is characterized by
floyd.explain: Full adder: 3 inputs (A, B, Cin), 2 outputs (Σ, Cout).
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #2
floyd.detail: Compared with a half-adder, a full-adder gains exactly 1 extra input (Cin), but the number of outputs stays at 2 (Σ, Cout). This is an easy detail to misremember: many people assume a full-adder also has more outputs, but only the input count actually increases.

floyd.q: The inputs to a full adder are A=1, B=0, Cin=1. The outputs are
floyd.explain: 1+0+1 = 10₂ (decimal 2) → sum bit Σ = 0, carry Cout = 1.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #3
floyd.detail: A quick method for any full-adder combination: simply add A+B+Cin as ordinary arithmetic (1+0+1=2), then convert that result to a 2-bit binary value (2=10₂). The low bit of that binary value is always Σ, and the high bit is always Cout.

floyd.q: A 3-bit parallel adder can add
floyd.explain: An n-bit parallel adder adds two n-bit numbers at the same time; with n = 3 → it adds two 3-bit numbers.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #4
floyd.detail: 'Parallel' in the name refers to ALL the bits of both numbers being presented at once on separate wires, unlike a serial adder, which processes one bit at a time over several clock cycles. An n-bit parallel adder always adds exactly two n-bit numbers.

floyd.q: To expand a 2-bit parallel adder to a 4-bit parallel adder, you must
opts: use two 2-bit adders and connect the sum outputs of one to the bit inputs of the other
use two 2-bit adders with no interconnections
use four 2-bit adders with no interconnections
use two 2-bit adders with the carry output of one connected to the carry input of the other
floyd.explain: Cascading by connecting the carry-out of the lower stage to the carry-in of the higher stage is the principle of the ripple-carry adder.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #5
floyd.detail: The principle for widening an adder is always the same: connect the Cout of the LOWER stage to the Cin of the next HIGHER stage, so the carry 'ripples' from low to high exactly the way manual addition works. Chaining two 2-bit adders this way forms exactly one complete 4-bit adder.

floyd.q: If a 74HC85 magnitude comparator has A=1000 and B=1010, the outputs are
floyd.explain: A = 8, B = 10 → A<B is true (=1), A>B is false (=0), A=B is false (=0).
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #6
floyd.detail: Before checking a comparator IC's truth table, it helps to convert the binary numbers to decimal for an intuitive comparison first: 1000=8 and 1010=10, so clearly 8<10. From there, it follows directly which output is active (A

floyd.q: If a 1-of-16 decoder with active-LOW outputs exhibits a LOW on the decimal 12 output, what are the inputs?
floyd.explain: 12 decimal = 1100 binary.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #7
floyd.detail: For a decoder question, always convert the decimal output number to its corresponding binary code on the address lines A3A2A1A0 before comparing against the options. Decimal 12 converts to the 4-bit binary value 1100, matching one of the options directly without needing any further reasoning about the IC's internal operation.

floyd.q: A BCD-to-7 segment decoder has 0100 on its inputs. The active outputs are
floyd.explain: 0100₂ = 4 decimal; displaying the digit 4 on a 7-segment LED needs segments b, c, f and g lit.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #8
floyd.detail: This problem combines two steps: converting the input BCD code to a decimal digit (0100=4), then checking the 7-segment convention table to see which segments that digit needs lit. The digit 4 on a 7-segment display has a distinctive shape lighting only 4 of the 7 segments (b, c, f, g), leaving a, d, e unlit.

floyd.q: If an octal-to-binary priority encoder has its 0,2,5,6 inputs active, the active-HIGH binary output is
floyd.explain: Select the input with the HIGHEST index among the active inputs {0, 2, 5, 6} → 6 is selected → binary code 110.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #9
floyd.detail: The core difference of a PRIORITY encoder versus an ordinary one: when SEVERAL inputs are active at once, it only encodes the input with the HIGHEST number, ignoring the other active inputs with lower numbers. With {0,2,5,6} all active, the highest number is 6, which converts to the 3-bit binary value 110.

floyd.q: In general, a multiplexer has
opts: several data inputs, several data outputs, and selection inputs
one data input, several data outputs, and selection inputs
several data inputs, one data output, and selection inputs
one data input, one data output, and one selection input
floyd.explain: The definition of a multiplexer: many inputs, 1 output, selected by the select lines.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #10
floyd.detail: A multiplexer's standard structure always follows the 'many-in, one-out' pattern: several data input lines, a single data output line, and a separate set of SELECT lines determining which input line connects to the output at any given moment.

floyd.q: Data distributors are basically the same as
floyd.explain: 'Data distributor' is another name for a demultiplexer.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #11
floyd.detail: The name 'data distributor' describes a demultiplexer's function from another angle: it DISTRIBUTES a single incoming data stream to exactly one of several destinations, similar to how a parcel distribution centre sends each package to its correct recipient address.

floyd.q: Which of the following codes exhibit even parity?
floyd.explain: 10011000 has three 1s (odd). 01111000 has four 1s (even) ✓. 11111111 has eight 1s (even) ✓. 11010101 has five 1s (odd). So only (b) and (c) have even parity.
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.6: Functions of Combinational Logic · Self-Test #12
floyd.detail: Checking even parity always works the same way: count the 1 bits across the whole code; an even count satisfies even parity, an odd count does not. Among the four codes in the question, only 2 of them, (b) and (c), have an even count of 1 bits, so the correct answer must select BOTH, not just a single code.
